chapters.name: Chapter 1: Setting up your coaching assistant

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What an AI coaching assistant can do
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: List coaching tasks to give to AI and decisions to keep for yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of weekly coaching tasks, you will list which coaching tasks to give an AI assistant to draft and which decisions to keep for yourself, keeping playing time, selection and safety decisions with the coach.
An AI coaching assistant is a general AI assistant, like ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot or Google Gemini, that you use for coaching work. It can draft practice plans, write emails, explain rules, create drill descriptions, quizzes and schedules, and summarize notes.
It cannot see your players, know their health or feelings, or take responsibility. Playing time, discipline, injury and return-to-play decisions, safety calls and anything about a player's wellbeing stay with you and the right professionals.
A good rule: AI drafts, the coach decides. Everything it writes is a first draft you check.
Words to know:
- AI coaching assistant: a general AI assistant used to help with coaching tasks.
- Return to play: the decision on when an injured athlete can safely play again; made by medical professionals.
Try it now: Write two lists: five weekly coaching tasks you could give AI to draft, and five decisions you will always keep.
You can now decide which coaching tasks AI can help with and which decisions stay human.

check.q: Which coaching task can AI draft for you?
options: Whether an injured player can return
check.why: AI can draft plans; selection, injuries and feelings need the coach and trained staff.

check.q: AI suggests benching a player based on your notes. What do you do?
options: Make the decision yourself from what you have seen
Ask AI again until it agrees
check.why: AI drafts, the coach decides, especially about playing time.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Writing standing instructions
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write standing instructions that tell the AI about your team and rules.
This lesson builds toward: For your own team, you will write standing instructions with the team level, practice length, style and safety rules, including a rule never to use player names or health details.
Standing instructions are a paragraph you paste at the start of a chat (or save in the assistant's custom instructions or project feature, if it has one) so it always knows your context.
Include: sport, level and age group; team size; practice length and facilities; your coaching style and values; safety rules (age-appropriate drills, water breaks, no punishment conditioning); and what it must never include (player names, health details, grades).
Example: "I coach a U12 girls' soccer team of 16 players. Practices are 90 minutes on half a field, Tuesdays and Thursdays. I value effort, fun and teamwork. Plans must include warm-up, water breaks every 20 minutes and age-appropriate drills. Never ask for or use player names or health details."
Step by step:
- Write your sport, level, age group and team size.
- Add practice length and facilities.
- Add your values and coaching style.
- Add safety rules.
- Add what it must never include.
- Save it where you can paste it each time.
Words to know:
- Standing instructions: context you give an AI at the start so every answer fits your situation.
- Age-appropriate: suitable for the age and development of the players.
Try it now: Write your standing instructions in one paragraph and save them in a note. Paste them into an AI assistant and ask: "Summarize what you know about my team." Fix anything it got wrong.
You can now write standing instructions that make AI answers fit your team.

options: A list of player phone numbers
Context about your team and rules that you give AI at the start
check.why: Standing instructions make every AI answer fit your team.

check.q: AI's summary of your standing instructions says your team is under-16, but it is under-12. What do you do?
options: Fix the instructions so it has the right age group
check.why: Wrong context gives wrong plans, so you correct it first.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Planning a practice with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a 90-minute practice plan and adjust it.
This lesson builds toward: Using your standing instructions, you will draft a 90-minute practice plan with AI and adjust it, so times add up, drills fit the age group and equipment, and at least two changes are made.
With your standing instructions pasted, ask: "Plan a 90-minute practice focused on [skill]. Include warm-up, three progressive drills, a small-sided game, cool-down and water breaks. Give times, setup, coaching points and how to make each drill easier or harder."
Check it like a coach: Are the drills safe and age-appropriate? Do the times add up? Do you have the space and equipment? Is the work-to-rest balance right? Are there too many lines and too much standing around?
Ask follow-ups: "We only have 10 balls." "Two players are new." "Swap drill 2 for something with more touches." Keep plans you like in a folder to reuse and improve.
Step by step:
- Paste your standing instructions.
- Ask for a 90-minute plan with times, setup and coaching points.
- Check safety, timing, space and equipment.
- Ask follow-ups to fix problems.
- Save the final plan.
Words to know:
- Progression: drills that build from simple to harder.
- Small-sided game: a game with fewer players and a smaller space so everyone gets more touches.
Try it now: Use your standing instructions to get a 90-minute practice plan for a real upcoming practice. Make at least two follow-up changes and save it.
You can now plan a safe, well-timed practice with AI help.

check.q: What is a progression in a practice plan?
options: Drills that build from simple to harder
check.why: A progression builds skills step by step.

check.q: AI's plan needs 20 cones and you have 8. What do you do?
options: Tell AI you have 8 cones and ask it to adjust
check.why: Give AI your real limits so the plan works on the field.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Messages to parents and players
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a clear, kind parent or player message with AI and send it through approved channels.
This lesson builds toward: Given a schedule change or team news, you will write a clear, kind parent or player message with AI and send it through an approved channel, with every date checked and nothing about one player in a group message.
Coaches write lots of messages: schedules, changes, reminders, expectations. Ask: "Write a short, friendly message to parents about next week's practice changes: Tuesday moves to 5 pm, Thursday is canceled for the field repair. Include what to bring. Under 100 words."
Check facts, dates and tone. Keep group messages about the team; never discuss one player's performance, health or behavior in a group message.
Use your school's or club's approved communication method. Many organizations have rules for coaches messaging minors, for example including a parent or another coach. Hard conversations, like playing time or behavior, are better in person or by phone, not AI-written texts.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a short, friendly draft.
- Check facts, dates and tone.
- Keep group messages about the team.
- Send through approved channels.
- Handle hard conversations in person.
Words to know:
- Approved channel: the communication method your school or club allows for coaches.
- Tone: how a message feels: friendly, firm, warm.
Try it now: Use AI to write a real or practice parent message about a schedule change. Check every date and send it (or save it) through your approved channel.
You can now write clear team messages with AI and send them the right way.

check.q: What should a team group message be about?
options: The team, such as times and places
check.why: Group messages are for team news; one player's issues are private.

check.q: AI writes a parent message that says practice is on Tuesday the 14th. What do you do before sending?
options: Send it from your personal account to the players only
Check the date on the calendar
check.why: AI can get dates wrong, so you check every date.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Drill cards and playbook quizzes
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create a drill card and a five-question playbook quiz.
This lesson builds toward: Given one drill and one play, you will create a drill card and a five-question playbook quiz with AI, with every step and answer checked against your real drill and play.
Drill cards help assistant coaches and players run drills the same way. Ask: "Make a one-page drill card for [drill]: purpose, setup, steps, coaching points, common mistakes, and how to make it easier or harder." Add a simple diagram in a tool like Canva or by hand.
Quizzes help players learn the playbook and rules. Ask: "Write five multiple-choice questions about our out-of-bounds play: [describe it]. One correct answer each, with a short explanation." Check every answer against your real play.
Use a quiz tool like Google Forms to share it, without collecting more personal information than needed.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for a drill card with purpose, setup, steps and coaching points.
- Add a simple diagram.
- Describe a play and ask for five quiz questions.
- Check every answer against your real play.
- Share with a simple form, collecting minimal info.
Words to know:
- Drill card: a one-page guide that explains how to run a drill.
- Playbook: a team's set of plays and rules for how to run them.
Try it now: Make one drill card and a five-question quiz on one of your plays with AI. Check both and fix anything wrong.
You can now create drill cards and playbook quizzes with AI help.

check.q: What does a drill card help with?
options: Running a drill the same way every time
check.why: A drill card gives purpose, setup, steps and coaching points so everyone runs it the same way.

check.q: One answer in AI's playbook quiz does not match your real play. What do you do?
options: Remove the quiz from the course
check.why: Every quiz answer must match how your team really runs the play.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Guardrails: privacy, safety and fairness
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write your coaching AI guardrails and follow them.
This lesson builds toward: Before using AI for any coaching task, you will write and follow guardrails for privacy, safety and fairness, sending medical and heat questions to trained staff and governing-body guidance.
Privacy: never paste player names with health information, injuries, grades, family situations, contact details or photos of minors into AI tools. Use positions or numbers. Check your organization's rules about which tools may be used with student or player data.
Safety: AI may suggest outdated or unsafe drills, conditioning or heat practices. Check drills against your governing body's guidance and your athletic trainer, and never use AI for medical, concussion or return-to-play decisions; the CDC's free HEADS UP training is one place to learn concussion basics.
Fairness and honesty: decisions about selection and playing time come from what you observe, explained to players in person. Be open with families that you use AI for planning, if your organization asks.
Step by step:
- Write your privacy rule: no names with private info.
- Write your safety rule: check drills; no medical decisions.
- Write your fairness rule: decisions from observation, explained in person.
- Check your organization's technology rules.
- Share the guardrails with your staff.
Words to know:
- Guardrail: a rule that keeps you safe while using a tool.
- Governing body: the organization that sets rules for your sport or level.
Official sources:
- CDC: HEADS UP concussion training
Try it now: Final task: write your guardrails and standing instructions, then produce a practice plan, a parent message, a drill card and a quiz with AI, checking each and confirming no private athlete data was used.
You can now use an AI coaching assistant with clear guardrails for privacy, safety and fairness.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Standing instructions Missing the team level, practice length or safety rules. Team level, length, style, safety rules and a no-private-data rule. Also lists equipment and space so plans fit the real field. Practice plan Times do not add up to 90 minutes or a drill is unsafe for the age group. A 90-minute plan with correct times and safe drills, changed at least twice. Has a clear progression and water breaks, and notes why each change was made. Parent message Wrong dates, an unkind tone, or private player details. Short, friendly, dates checked, sent or saved through an approved channel. Also includes who to contact with questions, following rules for messaging minors. Drill card and quiz A step or quiz answer does not match the real drill or play. Drill card with purpose, setup, steps and coaching points; five checked quiz questions. Quiz collects no more information than needed and covers the play's key moments. Guardrails and privacy A prompt includes player names or health details, or AI made a coach's decision. Written guardrails followed; no private athlete data used; decisions kept by the coach. Guardrails also say where medical and heat questions go. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What is a coaching AI guardrail?
options: A rule that keeps you safe while using AI
check.why: Guardrails set what you will and will not do with AI.

check.q: You want AI's help with a player's concussion recovery. What do you do?
check.why: Return-to-play decisions after a concussion belong to medical professionals.
